summary: A proposal for an experiment with a Message Switching Protocol (MSP), a system whose job is to switch messages among its ports. Written by Bob Bressler, Dan Murphy and Dave Walden, it gives a specification, message header format, examples and a Telnet-based information operator. It was categorized as experimentation and obsoletes RFC 62.

eli5.summary: Think of a switchboard operator who passes messages between many phone lines. This note suggests an experiment to build such a message-passing switchboard for computers on the network.

subtitle: An alternative network architecture using message switching instead of streams

tldr.problem: The then-current NCP architecture in the ARPANET emphasized stream-based communication, but researchers believed that message-switching—routing individual messages based on ports and rendezvous points—would be simpler and more flexible for host software.
tldr.mechanism: MSP uses SEND and RECEIVE operations where processes specify source and destination port IDs and a rendezvous host. Messages are buffered and switched by intermediate hosts until sender and receiver match, creating multiple rendezvous topologies (at sender, receiver, or intermediate host).
tldr.outcome: This proposal outlined an experimental message-switching protocol, requesting permission to run a limited experiment on reserved links 192-195 of the ARPANET.

today: RFC 333 proposes an experimental message-switching protocol that was never widely adopted. The stream-based architecture of existing NCPs remained standard, though message-switching concepts influenced later network protocol designs.

sections.title: Message Switching vs. Stream Orientation
sections.content:
RFC 333 proposes an experiment with a Message Switching Protocol (MSP), a fundamentally different approach to network communication. The authors—Bob Bressler, Dan Murphy, Dave Walden and collaborators—believe the stream-oriented design of existing NCPs reflects a reluctance to move away from traditional communications thinking. They propose rethinking the lowest-level host-host protocol around message switching principles.

Bressler had already implemented a message-switched system for the MIT Dynamic Modeling PDP-10 that was an order of magnitude smaller than his NCP, suggesting the approach could be simpler for host software to implement and manage.
sections.eli5: Right now network programs stay connected like a phone call. The note suggests trying a mail-delivery system where messages wait until both sides are ready.

sections.title: SEND, RECEIVE, and Rendezvous
sections.content:
In MSP, communication begins when a sending process executes SEND and a receiving process executes RECEIVE. Both specify port IDs (source and destination) and a rendezvous host. The SEND creates an OUT message with data, while RECEIVE creates an IN message. At the rendezvous host, when a matching OUT and IN are found, the OUT message and data are forwarded to the receiver, and the IN is forwarded to the sender. By varying which host is chosen as the rendezvous point, four different communication topologies are possible: rendezvous at sender, at receiver, at an intermediate host, or with both processes specifying the same rendezvous host.

This design separates process identification from the communication mechanism itself, allowing flexible routing and message buffering at intermediate hosts.
sections.eli5: A sender packages up a message and says 'meet at host C'. A receiver also says 'I'm ready at host C'. Host C matches them up and forwards the message to the receiver's host and an acknowledgment back to the sender.

sections.title: Message Format and Design Details
sections.content:
Each MSP message begins with a 144-bit header containing the destination (rendezvous host), port IDs (source and destination), message type (IN, OUT, FLUSH), bit count, and table position information. The header was carefully aligned so that fields do not cross word boundaries on 16, 32, and 36-bit word machines, easing implementation at the interrupt level.

Port IDs are 24 bits, with the first 8 bits designating the host where the port was created. The protocol allows wildcard ports (all zeros) for flexible send/receive patterns. Links 192-195 are reserved for the MSP experiment to run in parallel with the existing protocol.
sections.eli5: The message header has all the address information: who sent it, who should get it, where they meet, and how big the message is, all packed so that computer hardware can read it efficiently.

sections.title: Design Rationale and Trade-offs
sections.content:
RFC 333 discusses several design choices and open issues. Timeouts are noted as complex: many hosts cannot support them, yet without them, negative acknowledgments (FLUSH messages) risk races. The protocol allows hosts to discard messages they cannot buffer, avoiding deadlock. Process blocking after SEND/RECEIVE is left implementation-dependent, and multiple simultaneous messages between the same ports are allowed if applications handle sequencing.

The authors believe message switching offers advantages in simplicity and flexibility compared to stream-based NCPs. They welcome comments from the network working group on this experimental proposal but reserve the right to reject suggestions since this is a limited experiment, not a replacement for the current protocol.
sections.eli5: The design has to handle tricky cases like what happens if a message gets lost, or if a computer can't store a message. The note leaves these decisions to each site so they can tune for their needs.
